public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Lovász–Plummer conjecture (proved 2011) and Sheehan's conjecture

*References:*
* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersen%27s_theorem#Related_conjectures)
* [LP86] Lovász, L. and Plummer, M. D. (1986). *Matching Theory.* North-Holland.
* [EKKKN11] Esperet, L., Kardoš, F., King, A. D., Král', D. and Norine, S. (2011).
  "Exponentially many perfect matchings in cubic graphs." *Adv. Math.* 227, pp. 1646--1664.
  [arXiv:1012.2878](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2878)
* [Sh77] Sheehan, J. (1977). "The multiplicity of Hamiltonian circuits in a graph." In *Recent
  Advances in Graph Theory*, Academia, Prague, pp. 477--480.
* [Th98] Thomassen, C. (1998). "Independent dominating sets and a second Hamiltonian cycle in
  regular graphs." *J. Combin. Theory Ser. B* 72, pp. 104--109.
-/

@[expose] public section

open SimpleGraph

namespace LovaszPlummerConjecture

variable {V : Type*}

/-- The number of perfect matchings of `G`. -/
noncomputable def perfectMatchingCount (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  {M : G.Subgraph | M.IsPerfectMatching}.ncard

/--
**The Lovász–Plummer conjecture (1970s), proved by Esperet, Kardoš, King, Král' and Norine
(2011).**

Every bridgeless cubic graph on $n$ vertices has exponentially many perfect matchings: there is
a constant $c > 0$ such that the number of perfect matchings is at least $2^{cn}$.
[EKKKN11] prove this with $2^{n/3656}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem lovasz_plummer_conjecture :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
      (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      (∀ v, G.degree v = 3) → G.IsBridgeless →
      (2 : ℝ) ^ (c * Fintype.card V) ≤ perfectMatchingCount G := by
  sorry

/--
**The explicit bound of Esperet–Kardoš–King–Král'–Norine (2011).**

Every bridgeless cubic graph on $n$ vertices has at least $2^{n/3656}$ perfect matchings.

*Reference:* [EKKKN11].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem lovasz_plummer_conjecture.variants.explicit
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hcubic : ∀ v, G.degree v = 3) (hbridgeless : G.IsBridgeless) :
    (2 : ℝ) ^ ((Fintype.card V : ℝ) / 3656) ≤ perfectMatchingCount G := by
  sorry

/-- A **Hamiltonian cycle** of `G`: a cycle passing through every vertex. -/
def IsHamiltonianCycle (G : SimpleGraph V) {v : V} (c : G.Walk v v) : Prop :=
  c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ w, w ∈ c.support

/--
**Sheehan's conjecture (1977).**

Every $4$-regular graph with a Hamiltonian cycle has a second Hamiltonian cycle (one with a
different edge set). Sheehan's conjecture would settle the last open case of the question,
raised by Smith's theorem for cubic graphs, of which regular Hamiltonian graphs have a second
Hamiltonian cycle: Thomassen [Th98] proved it for all $r$-regular graphs with $r \ge 300$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem sheehan_conjecture :
    ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      (∀ v, G.degree v = 4) →
      ∀ (v : V) (c : G.Walk v v), IsHamiltonianCycle G c →
        ∃ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), IsHamiltonianCycle G c' ∧
          c'.edges.toFinset ≠ c.edges.toFinset := by
  sorry

/--
**Thomassen (1998): regular graphs of large degree.**

Every $r$-regular Hamiltonian graph with $r \ge 300$ has a second Hamiltonian cycle.

*Reference:* [Th98].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem sheehan_conjecture.variants.thomassen
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (r : ℕ) (hr : 300 ≤ r) (hreg : ∀ v, G.degree v = r)
    (v : V) (c : G.Walk v v) (hc : IsHamiltonianCycle G c) :
    ∃ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), IsHamiltonianCycle G c' ∧
      c'.edges.toFinset ≠ c.edges.toFinset := by
  sorry

end LovaszPlummerConjecture

findings.description: The module docstring's only Wikipedia reference is `https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersen%27s_theorem#Related_conjectures`. That article has no 'Related conjectures' section. I checked the current revision (1298007007, 2025-06-29) and sampled revisions back to 2015. The Lovász–Plummer material is under 'Extensions › Number of perfect matchings in cubic bridgeless graphs'. The article never mentions Sheehan's conjecture, the second-Hamiltonian-cycle question or Thomassen's theorem. So `sheehan_conjecture` and `sheehan_conjecture.variants.thomassen` get no support from the cited Wikipedia page, although the file sits in `FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/`. The Lean statements themselves are faithful to the literature (see the other sources).
findings.source_evidence: Raw wikitext of https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Petersen%27s_theorem&action=raw has these headings only: Proof, History, Applications, Extensions (Each edge belongs to some perfect matching…, Number of perfect matchings in cubic bridgeless graphs, Algorithmic versions, Higher degree), See also, Notes, References. Neither 'Sheehan' nor 'Related conjectures' occurs in this or older revisions (e.g. oldid 1178561266, 1042426618, 908160102, 652107690). A Wikipedia full-text search for "Sheehan's conjecture" returns 0 hits.

(arXiv:1812.05650); or Haxell–Seamone–Verstraëte, JGT 54 (2007).

findings.description: The docstring title says "Sheehan's conjecture (1977)". The module reference `[Sh77] Sheehan, J. (1977). "The multiplicity of Hamiltonian circuits in a graph." In Recent Advances in Graph Theory, Academia, Prague, pp. 477--480` also gives 1977. That paper is from the Second Czechoslovak Symposium (Prague, June 1974) and was published in 1975. Sheehan's 1977 paper is a different one: 'Graphs with exactly one hamiltonian circuit', J. Graph Theory 1 (1977) 37–43, about the maximum size of uniquely Hamiltonian graphs. Only the date is wrong; the mathematics is not affected.
findings.source_evidence: zbMATH Zbl 0327.05116: 'The multiplicity of Hamiltonian circuits in a graph', source 'Recent Adv. Graph Theory, Proc. Symp. Prague 1974, 477-480 (1975)', year 1975. arXiv:1812.05650 recalls 'a conjecture of Sheehan from 1974' and cites it as 1975. arXiv:2304.08946 cites it as 'Proceedings of the Second Czechoslovak Symposium, Prague, 1974), 477--480, 1975'. Girão–Kittipassorn–Narayanan (arXiv:1709.04895) say 'a well-known conjecture of Sheehan from 1975'.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel the reference as `[Sh75] Sheehan, J. (1975)`, noting the Proc. 2nd Czechoslovak Symposium, Prague 1974. Change the docstring title to "Sheehan's conjecture (1975)".

reformulations.difference: The Lean quantifies only over `SimpleGraph`s. The source setting includes cubic bridgeless multigraphs: EKKKN 'allow graphs to have multiple edges, but not loops', and LP86 also allows them. A reader might therefore take the Lean for a weaker special case.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A cubic bridgeless graph has no loops: the third edge at a looped vertex would be a bridge. Parallel edges occur in only two forms. (1) A 2-vertex triple-edge component, with m = 3. Replace it by K4, which also has m = 3. (2) A digon u=v with third edges a–u and v–b. Here a ≠ b, since otherwise a's third edge is a bridge. Replace the digon by a diamond K4−e with degree-2 vertices p, q joined to a and b. Parity forces both port edges to be used or neither. With neither used, the diamond has exactly 2 internal perfect matchings; with both used, exactly 1 (xy). These are the digon's local counts (2 parallel choices, or 1). The resulting G' is simple, cubic and bridgeless, with m(G') = m(G) and |V(G')| ≥ |V(G)|. So m(G) = m(G') ≥ 2^{c|V(G')|} ≥ 2^{c|V(G)|}. The simple-graph statement therefore implies the multigraph statement with the same c; the converse is trivial. The two are equivalent. The statement also matches EKKKN's form of the conjecture: ∃ ε > 0 with 2^{ε|V(G)|} ≤ |M(G)|.

reformulations.difference: The Lean covers simple cubic bridgeless graphs only. EKKKN's Theorem 1 (m(G) ≥ 2^{|V(G)|/3656}) is proved for loopless multigraphs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same diamond / K4 gadget replacement turns any cubic bridgeless multigraph into a simple cubic bridgeless graph. It preserves the number of perfect matchings and does not decrease the number of vertices. So the bound with the constant 1/3656 transfers exactly, and the converse is trivial.

reformulations.difference: The source says 'there is no uniquely hamiltonian 4-regular graph', i.e. every hamiltonian 4-regular graph has a second hamiltonian cycle. The Lean encodes cycles as based closed walks, using a file-local `IsHamiltonianCycle` (`c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ w, w ∈ c.support`). 'Second' is expressed as a Hamiltonian closed walk whose `edges.toFinset` differs from that of c. The same encoding is used in `sheehan_conjecture.variants.thomassen`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: I proved in Lean that the file-local `IsHamiltonianCycle G c` is equivalent to Mathlib's `c.IsHamiltonianCycle`. A Hamiltonian cycle, as a subgraph, is determined by its edge set. The closed walks representing one cycle (rotations and the reversal) have the same edge finset; I proved this for `Walk.reverse` and `Walk.rotate`. Hence 'there is a Hamiltonian closed walk with a different edge finset' holds exactly when G has at least two Hamiltonian cycles. `SimpleGraph` is the correct setting: Fleischner (JGT 1994) built 4-regular uniquely hamiltonian multigraphs.

review.notes:
No mathematical defects found. All four theorem statements match their sources.

- **`lovasz_plummer_conjecture` and `.variants.explicit`:** these match EKKKN (arXiv:1012.2878, Theorem 1: m(G) ≥ 2^{|V(G)|/3656}) and Wikipedia. They are correctly tagged solved.
- **`sheehan_conjecture` and `.variants.thomassen`:** these match the zbMATH review of Thomassen 1998 almost word for word: 'every hamiltonian r-regular graph for r ≥ 300 has a second hamiltonian cycle', and 'Sheehan: every hamiltonian 4-regular graph has a second hamiltonian cycle'. They are correctly tagged open and solved respectively. The latest literature I found (arXiv:2304.08946, v2 Nov 2024) still treats Sheehan's conjecture as open. arXiv searches up to Sep 2026 show no resolution.

**Definitions checked:**
- `perfectMatchingCount`: counts `G.Subgraph`s with `IsPerfectMatching`. Perfect matchings have verts = univ, so these are in bijection with perfect-matching edge sets. I proved in Lean that the set is finite, so `ncard` is not the junk value 0. Also checked: count = 1 for the empty graph (the n = 0 case of the inequality holds) and count = 1 for K2.
- `IsBridgeless`: quantifies only over actual edges. This matters because Mathlib's `IsBridge` no longer includes adjacency.
- `IsHamiltonianCycle`: proved equivalent to Mathlib's `Walk.IsHamiltonianCycle`.

**Docstring remark (not filed as a finding):** the `sheehan_conjecture` docstring says the conjecture 'would settle the last open case' and cites only Thomassen's r ≥ 300. Since Haxell–Seamone–Verstraëte (2007, r > 22), the open cases are all even r with 4 ≤ r ≤ 22. All of them follow from the r = 4 case via Petersen's 2-factor theorem. The remark is outdated but not false.

**Sources I could not read directly:** Sheehan (1975) and Thomassen (1998) are print-only or captcha-protected. The statements were checked through the zbMATH review and the GMZ and 2304.08946 papers. I read LP86 Conjecture 8.1.8 only as quoted in EKKKN: it is the k-regular matching-covered generalization, and its k = 3 case is the conjecture stated here.
